lesson.title: Encapsulation: Bundling Data and Behavior Together
lesson.summary: Encapsulation is the object-oriented practice of packaging an object's data together with the methods that operate on it, and using those methods as the intended, controlled way to interact with that data.
lesson.body:
Object-oriented programming rests on the idea that data and the behavior that makes sense of it belong together. A circle's radius and the method that computes its area aren't really separate concerns, they're two halves of one coherent idea, and a class is what lets you bundle them into a single unit. That bundling is the first half of what's called encapsulation: instead of scattering related data and functions across your program and hoping you always use them correctly together, you package them into one class, where they travel as a set.

The second half of encapsulation builds on abstraction, the idea that users of an object shouldn't need to know its internal details to use it correctly, only its outward behavior. Encapsulation takes that further by actively steering how outside code interacts with an object's data, funneling changes through methods that can check, adjust, or reject a change, rather than letting any code reach in and set an attribute directly to anything at all.

```python
class Thermostat:
    def __init__(self, temperature):
        self.temperature = temperature

    def set_temperature(self, new_temp):
        if 60 <= new_temp <= 80:
            self.temperature = new_temp
        else:
            print("Temperature must be between 60 and 80.")

t = Thermostat(70)
t.set_temperature(85)
print(t.temperature)
# Output:
# Temperature must be between 60 and 80.
# 70

t.set_temperature(72)
print(t.temperature)
# Output: 72
```

Follow the trace closely. t starts with temperature 70. Calling t.set_temperature(85) checks 60 <= 85 <= 80, which is false since 85 is above 80, so the method prints its warning message and leaves self.temperature untouched at 70; the very next print(t.temperature) confirms that by showing 70. Calling t.set_temperature(72) checks 60 <= 72 <= 80, which is true, so self.temperature is updated to 72, and print(t.temperature) now shows 72. The set_temperature method is doing real work here: it's the gatekeeper that keeps the object in a sensible state.

There's an honest catch worth naming right away, because overclaiming it would be misleading: nothing in this Thermostat class actually stops outside code from writing t.temperature = 999 directly, completely bypassing set_temperature's range check. In Python, encapsulation as shown here is a design pattern and a convention for good, safe interfaces, not a wall enforced by the language. The next chapter, on private attributes, looks at how Python programmers signal (and partially protect) which attributes are meant to be touched only through methods like this one.
